stories.title: The new GPT-5.6 family: Luna, Terra, Sol
stories.summary:
↳ WHAT'S NEW
OpenAI's GPT-5.6 family launches in general availability with three tiers: Luna ($1/$6 per 1M input/output tokens), Terra ($2.50/$15), and Sol ($5/$30).

↳ THE REAL STORY
The pricing is the headline here. Sol, the largest model, undercuts Claude Opus ($5/$25) on input cost while matching it — and beats Claude Fable 5 ($10/$50) by half on both dimensions. For teams running high-volume inference, Luna at $1 input is aggressive: a million-token context window costs a dollar to fill. That changes the calculus on tasks previously reserved for smaller, cheaper models. If quality holds up at the Luna tier, a lot of Claude Haiku and GPT-4o-mini workloads get re-evaluated this week.
stories.considerations: Three model names in one family is a support and versioning headache waiting to happen. 'Luna', 'Terra', 'Sol' are memorable in a press release and confusing in a codebase six months from now — especially if OpenAI follows its usual pattern of quietly updating model weights without bumping the name. The deeper question: the excerpt cuts off mid-comparison, so we don't have output quality benchmarks yet. Price leadership means nothing if Terra underperforms Claude Opus on reasoning tasks that justify the spend. Wait for independent evals before routing anything critical.

stories.title: [AINews] OpenAI launches GPT 5.6 Sol/Terra/Luna, Codex becomes ChatGPT superapp
stories.summary:
↳ WHAT'S NEW
OpenAI launched GPT 5.6 in three variants — Sol, Terra, and Luna — and repositioned Codex as the foundation of a broader ChatGPT superapp strategy.

↳ THE REAL STORY
The three-variant structure suggests OpenAI is tiering by capability and cost rather than releasing a single monolithic model — likely meaning Sol sits at the lightweight/fast end, Luna at the high-capability end, with Terra somewhere in between. For developers, this matters immediately at the API level: model selection becomes a cost-routing decision, not just a quality one. The Codex-as-superapp move is the more structurally significant shift — folding code generation into ChatGPT's core surface rather than keeping it as a separate product signals that OpenAI wants ChatGPT to be the primary interface for software development workflows, not just a chat assistant that happens to write code.
stories.considerations: The three-model naming scheme (Sol/Terra/Luna) is clean marketing, but the real question is whether the capability gaps between variants are meaningful enough to justify the routing complexity — or whether this is mostly a pricing segmentation play dressed up as a model family. On the Codex superapp front: consolidating everything into ChatGPT grows the moat but also increases lock-in risk for teams that built workflows around the standalone Codex API. Watch for deprecation timelines on existing endpoints.

stories.title: Ways to think about token pricing
stories.summary:
↳ WHAT'S NEW
Benedict Evans published an analysis on token pricing economics — examining how AI model labs currently operate in a supply-constrained market and what equilibrium looks like when capacity catches up to demand.

↳ THE REAL STORY
The core argument: model labs are pricing like monopolists right now because GPU supply is genuinely scarce. But that's a temporary condition, not a structural moat. As capacity expands — driven by massive capex from hyperscalers and labs alike — the question becomes whether tokens commoditize the way cloud compute did. If inference becomes undifferentiated infrastructure, margin pressure follows the same path as EC2 pricing over the last decade: relentless downward drift. For developers building cost models into their products today, the bet is that token prices continue falling, which changes the math on what's worth building with AI versus what's too expensive to ship.
stories.considerations: The uncomfortable question Evans is circling: what actually differentiates one lab's tokens from another's at scale? If GPT-4o and Claude and Gemini converge on capability — which benchmarks increasingly suggest — then price and latency become the only levers. That's a race to the bottom for labs, but a genuine tailwind for builders. The catch is timing: labs are burning capital at a rate that requires premium pricing to survive long enough to reach that equilibrium. If a lab misprices the transition — too slow to cut, too fast to commoditize — it either bleeds out or gets stranded with underutilized capacity. Developers should watch whether labs start competing on price in the next 12 months as a leading indicator that the supply crunch is actually breaking.

stories.title: Introducing Muse Spark 1.1
stories.summary:
↳ WHAT'S NEW
Muse Spark 1.1 is Meta's first Spark model with an API, following the original Muse Spark release in April. Meta reports significant improvements in agentic tool calling and computer use capabilities.

↳ THE REAL STORY
The API availability is the meaningful shift here — Muse Spark was previously inaccessible to developers building production systems. If the agentic tool calling improvements hold up, this becomes a candidate for workflows that require multi-step reasoning with external tools or UI automation. Computer use support in particular puts it in direct competition with Anthropic's Claude and its operator-facing computer use API.
stories.considerations: The excerpt is thin on specifics — no benchmark numbers, no pricing, no context window details, and no clarity on what 'significant improvements' actually means in measurable terms. Until independent evals surface, treat the agentic claims as marketing copy. Worth watching whether Meta's API terms allow commercial use at scale, which has historically been a friction point with their model releases.

stories.title: llm 0.31.1
stories.summary:
↳ WHAT'S NEW
llm 0.31.1 patches a single bug: tool calls returning empty arguments from OpenAI Chat Completion endpoints were throwing JSON parse errors on certain providers.

↳ THE REAL STORY
If you're using llm with non-OpenAI providers that speak the OpenAI Chat Completion protocol — think local inference servers, Azure, or third-party wrappers — tool/function calling could silently break whenever a model returned an empty argument object. The fix is narrow but the failure mode was silent enough to waste real debugging time. Worth pulling the update if tool use is anywhere in your pipeline.
stories.considerations: The bug surfaced during Willison's own testing, which is a good sign for the project's quality loop — but it also flags that edge cases in tool-call argument handling are still shaking out across the OpenAI-compatible provider ecosystem. Empty arguments are a legitimate response when a tool takes no parameters; the fact that this slipped through suggests anyone building multi-provider tool-use workflows should be running their own integration tests against each provider, not assuming protocol compatibility means behavioral compatibility.
